subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Laniakea Supercluster
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Laniakea Supercluster.

hook.text: Our galaxy belongs to a supercluster of 100,000 galaxies called Laniakea—'immense heaven' in Hawaiian.

buildup.text: Laniakea spans 520 million light-years. All its galaxies flow toward a region called the Great Attractor.

discovery.text: Brent Tully's team mapped it in 2014 by tracking galaxy velocities. The flows revealed the supercluster's boundary.

twist.text: Superclusters aren't bound by gravity. Dark energy will eventually pull Laniakea apart over billions of years.

climax.text: The Great Attractor itself is a mass concentration hidden behind the Milky Way's dusty disk. We can only study it indirectly.

punchline.text: A hundred thousand galaxies flowing together. Our address in the cosmos.

quiz.question: What is the Great Attractor?
options: A massive gravitational concentration that galaxies in Laniakea flow toward
A supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way
A theoretical point where the Big Bang originated

details.summary: Laniakea (Hawaiian for 'immense heaven') is the supercluster that contains our Milky Way, spanning about 520 million light-years and containing roughly 100,000 galaxies.
details.whyItMatters: Laniakea defined our cosmic address at the largest scale and introduced a new way to map superclusters based on gravitational flow rather than just galaxy positions, reshaping our understanding of cosmic structure.
takeaways: Our supercluster, spanning about 520 million light-years
Contains roughly 100,000 galaxies including the Milky Way
Defined by shared gravitational flow toward the Great Attractor

faq.question: What is the Great Attractor?
faq.answer: A gravitational anomaly at the center of Laniakea, pulling galaxies toward it at hundreds of km/s. It lies about 250 million light-years away behind the plane of the Milky Way (the Zone of Avoidance). It's not a single massive object but a concentration of mass including several galaxy clusters.

faq.question: Is Laniakea gravitationally bound?
faq.answer: No. Unlike galaxy clusters, Laniakea is too large to resist the expansion of the universe (dark energy). Over time, its outer regions will be pulled apart by cosmic expansion. Only the dense inner structures (like the Virgo Cluster) are truly gravitationally bound and will survive indefinitely.
